blocks.content: Classic Shewhart {{term:regelkarte|charts}} ({{term:i-mr-chart|I-MR}}, {{term:xbar-r-chart|X̄-R}}) are insensitive to small persistent shifts — a 1σ drift is often only detected after 40–50 points. Time-weighted charts integrate information across multiple observations and pick up exactly those patterns much faster.

On the {{term:ewma-chart|EWMA chart}} each value is a weighted average of the current observation and the previous EWMA: zᵢ = λ·xᵢ + (1−λ)·zᵢ₋₁. The smoothing parameter λ controls memory: small λ (0.05–0.1) detects very small shifts, larger λ (0.3–0.4) behaves more like a Shewhart chart.

The {{term:cusum-chart|CUSUM chart}} accumulates the deviations from the target but counts only the part of a deviation that exceeds the reference value k. Two one-sided sums C⁺ and C⁻ detect upward and downward shifts. A signal fires as soon as either sum exceeds the decision interval h.

Both charts are used in the Control phase when a process is already running (target μ₀ and σ known) and small slow drifts must be detected early — typical use: chemical processes, tool wear, gauge drift.

items: Determine target μ₀ and spread σ from a stable baseline. In the module, set the baseline count to the length of that run or give target and σ; without a count the whole series counts as the baseline.
Prefer σ̂ from the average moving {{term:spannweite|range}} MR̄/d₂: because only consecutive values are compared, shifts and trends in the baseline inflate the estimate less than the sample SD.
Decide which shift size you want to detect early — e.g. 1σ.
EWMA: λ ≈ 0.1 for 1σ shifts; use L = 2.7 (instead of 3.0) when λ is small.
CUSUM: k = 0.5 and h = 4 or 5 (each in σ) — this combination detects a 1σ shift after about 8 (h = 4) or 10 points (h = 5) on average.
Run the chart and react to the first signal (point outside the limits).

blocks.content: Rule of thumb for shift size: to detect a Δ·σ shift, choose k = Δ/2 (in σ). The CUSUM procedure is then tuned optimally to that shift.

items: EWMA: the zᵢ line crosses UCL/LCL → {{term:sonderursache|special cause}}. The limits widen at the start (transient) and approach the steady-state asymptotically.
CUSUM: C⁺ rising → upward shift; C⁻ rising → downward shift. Signal as soon as either sum crosses the horizontal limit h.

Both charts report a shift only some points after its onset, because the deviation has to accumulate first — this costs reaction time but gains sensitivity to small shifts. For CUSUM the onset usually lies just after the last point at which the affected sum was 0.

After a signal: investigate the cause and correct the process. The module runs through the series without a restart; start the evaluation after the correction with a column that holds values only from the correction on.

blocks.content: If σ is computed from a sample with special causes, the limits are too wide. Always estimate from a confirmed-stable baseline — preferably from MR̄/d₂.

Without a baseline count and without given values, the module estimates target and σ from the whole series. If it already contains the shift, the target lies between the old and the new level: the chart reports the shift more weakly, and signals can appear before it in the opposite direction. Set the baseline count to the stable run or give target and σ.
EWMA is sluggish for large, sudden jumps. For single large outliers an {{term:i-mr-chart|I-MR chart}} reacts faster. Running EWMA and Shewhart in parallel is common (two-tier monitoring).

After a correction, C⁺ and C⁻ must start again at 0 — otherwise the old deviation keeps contributing to the next signal. The module does not reset the sums itself: evaluate the values from the correction on in a separate column.
Both methods assume independent observations. With autocorrelated data (batch processes, continuous measurements) they fire too many false alarms. Decorrelate first or use a model-residual chart.
Values other than the standard pairs (k = 0.5 with h = 4 or 5) drastically change the ARL behavior. If you deviate, consult ARL tables or run a simulation.
